content: Raphael House is a pioneering shelter located in the Tenderloin district of San Francisco, California. It provides transitional housing and support programs specifically designed for parents and children experiencing homelessness. Established in 1971 at the intersection of Gough and McAllister Streets, it was the first shelter in the city dedicated to homeless families. Since 1977, it has been situated on Sutter Street. This non-profit organization operates without government funding, relying instead on philanthropic contributions from the San Francisco Bay Area. These contributions have become increasingly innovative over time. However, not all offers of support are accepted. Between 1979 and 1999, Raphael House also ran Brother Juniper's Restaurant, an on-site breakfast café named after Saint Juniper. While the restaurant generated a modest net profit for two decades, it was eventually closed due to the high costs of renovating its kitchen and the need to repurpose the space for a children’s after-school tutorial center. The shelter was founded during a time when no other facilities for homeless families existed in the city. Its focus has always been on children, as evidenced by the brightly colored children’s paintings that adorn its hallways. The building itself exudes the warmth of an old-fashioned home, with braided rugs on the floors and flowered tablecloths in the dining rooms. Families residing at Raphael House commit to spending several months in a structured, nurturing environment. This includes adhering to curfews, following behavioral guidelines, and participating in counseling and practical training programs. Each of the approximately 20 families has its own small room, but much of daily life is communal, enriched by rituals that provide both stability and variety. Parents and children share breakfast and dinner together, seated as families. In the evenings, young children gather in the Children's Garden to listen to stories before being led, in their pajamas, in a singing procession to their rooms. During mid-winter, special visitors such as Santa Claus, St. Nicholas, and Santa Lucia bring gifts and treats to the children. Raphael House operates entirely on donations, supplemented by earnings from its thrift shop and the now-closed Brother Juniper's Restaurant. The shelter began in the basement of what was clearly a former hospital, navigating through piles of donated furniture and bins of bedding, which are later given to residents when they transition to their own homes. The shelter maintains strong ties to the Eastern Orthodox Church. Visitors often encounter bearded men in long black robes, including Father David Lowell, the Executive Director, who is a tall, lean priest. The day care center at Raphael House recently graduated its first class of licensed day care providers, consisting of four parents. Although the room was nearly empty during a visit—most children were on a field trip—a small girl who had just woken from her nap waved a juice bottle solemnly in the visitors' direction. The roof garden at Raphael House serves as a playground. The wooden deck is long enough for a six-year-old to run across, and large pots of plants are interspersed with playhouses and low climbing structures. In an area with limited open space, the children of Raphael House have the unique opportunity to play in the sky.
